beats.text: He was one of the most famous men in the world. Then his own government took away his passport, and tried to erase him.

overlays.hook: One of the most famous men alive. *Then America took his passport.*

beats.text: On June 12th, 1956, he sat in front of a committee of the United States Congress.
They asked about his politics, and about his travels. Then one of them asked why he did not just go and live in Russia.
He answered: Because my father was a slave, and my people died to build this country. And I am going to stay here, and have a part of it, just like you.

visual.quote: Because my father was a slave, and my people died to build this country, and I am going to stay here, and have a part of it just like you.

beats.text: His name was Paul Robeson. This is his story.
Paul Robeson was born on April 9th, 1898, in Princeton, New Jersey.
His father, William Drew Robeson, had been born into slavery in North Carolina. As a teenager, he escaped.
He went to school, and became the minister of a Black Presbyterian church in Princeton. After a dispute with the church's white backers, he lost that pulpit.
Then, when Paul was six years old, his mother died in a fire at home.

visual.title: Six years old
visual.sub: his mother died in a fire

beats.text: His father raised him alone, and expected the very best from him.
In 1915, Paul won a statewide exam, and a scholarship to Rutgers College.
He was only the third Black student ever to enroll there, and the only one at the time.

visual.caption: Robeson with Cap and Skull inductees, Rutgers, 1919

beats.text: He tried out for the football team. His own teammates did not want him. In the first scrimmages, they broke his nose, and dislocated his shoulder.
He came back anyway. And he became the best player on the field.
He was named an All-American twice. He earned varsity letters in four sports. He was elected to Phi Beta Kappa.
And in 1919, his classmates chose him as valedictorian. In his speech, he called for equality for every American.
Next came law school, at Columbia. To pay for it, he played professional football on weekends, for the Akron Pros, and the Milwaukee Badgers.
He was one of the first Black players in what became the N F L.
In 1921 he married Eslanda Goode, a chemist, who would later manage his career.
He graduated in 1923, and joined a law firm in New York.
But a white secretary there refused to take dictation from him, because he was Black.

visual.title: She refused
visual.sub: to take dictation from a Black man

beats.text: He walked out. Not just out of that job, but out of the law, for good.
So he turned to the stage. In 1924 he starred in two plays by Eugene O'Neill in New York, All God's Chillun Got Wings, and The Emperor Jones.
In 1925 he made his first film, Body and Soul, for the Black director Oscar Micheaux. He played two brothers: a crooked preacher, and an honest man.
That same year, with the pianist Lawrence Brown, he gave a concert of nothing but Black spirituals.
It was a sensation. His deep bass voice made him a star.
In 1928, he sang Ol' Man River in Show Boat, in London. It became his song for the rest of his life.
In 1930 he played Othello in London. A Black actor in that role was rare, and it made headlines.
The Robesons stayed in Britain for most of the next decade. He was rich, and famous across the world.
In 1933 he starred in the film of The Emperor Jones, a rare film of its time with a Black actor in the lead role.
In Britain, he got to know Welsh coal miners, and men fighting colonial rule in Africa and India. He began to see his own people's struggle as part of a bigger one.
In 1934 he visited the Soviet Union. He said that there, for the first time in his life, he felt like a full human being.

visual.quote: Here I am not a Negro but a human being for the first time in my life.

beats.text: In 1938 he went to Spain, in the middle of its civil war, to sing for the soldiers fighting fascism.
In 1939 he came home. On national radio, he sang Ballad for Americans, a song about what America could be. It was a hit.
During the war, he sang for workers in the shipyards.

visual.caption: Robeson leads shipyard workers in song, Oakland, 1942

beats.text: In 1943 he played Othello on Broadway. It ran 296 performances, still a record for Shakespeare on Broadway.
The N A A C P gave him its highest honor, the Spingarn Medal.
He was one of the most famous Black men in the world.
And he refused to stay quiet. In 1946, after a wave of lynchings, he led a delegation to the White House.
He asked President Truman to speak out against lynching. Truman said the time was not right.
Robeson warned that if the government would not protect Black Americans, they would defend themselves. The meeting was over.
He also kept praising the Soviet Union. In Cold War America, that made him a target.
In April 1949, he spoke at a peace congress in Paris. American newspapers reported that he had said Black Americans would never fight a war against Russia.
His words had been twisted. But the damage was done.
Congress even called in Jackie Robinson, the man who broke baseball's color line, to answer him.
Robinson said Robeson's statement, if it was reported right, sounded silly. And he used his time to attack racism at home.
That summer, Robeson was due to sing at a concert near Peekskill, New York.
Before he even got there, a mob attacked the crowd with rocks and clubs. A cross was burned on a hill nearby. The police did almost nothing.
A week later, he came back and sang to some twenty thousand people.
As they drove home, rioters stoned their cars and buses. More than a hundred and forty people were hurt.
In 1950, the State Department cancelled his passport. He could no longer travel, or perform, abroad.
To get it back, he was told to sign a statement promising not to make speeches overseas. He refused.
At home, he was blacklisted. Concert halls shut their doors. His records were pulled from stores. His films disappeared.
His income fell from over a hundred thousand dollars a year to almost nothing.
He kept speaking out anyway, beside friends like W. E. B. Du Bois.

visual.caption: Robeson, W. E. B. Du Bois and Vito Marcantonio, 1951

beats.text: In January 1952, a miners' union in Canada invited him to sing in Vancouver. No passport was needed to enter Canada back then.
He was stopped at the border anyway, and turned back.
So the union brought the concert to him. On May 18th, 1952, at the Peace Arch on the border, he stood on a flatbed truck on the American side.
And he sang across the line, to tens of thousands of people on both sides.
In 1957, he did it again, across an ocean. Over the new transatlantic telephone cable, he sang from New York to a hall full of Welsh miners.
And in 1956, Congress called him in. The House Un-American Activities Committee.
He refused to say whether he was a Communist. He told them his father was a slave, and that he would stay.
Then, before it was over, he told the committee: You are the un-Americans, and you ought to be ashamed of yourselves.

visual.quote: You are the un-Americans, and you ought to be ashamed of yourselves.

beats.text: In 1958 he published a book, Here I Stand. That June, the Supreme Court ruled that the government could not deny a passport over a person's beliefs.
After eight years, Paul Robeson got his passport back. He left for Europe almost at once.

visual.caption: Paul Robeson in The Emperor Jones, 1933

beats.text: In London he became the first Black performer to sing at Saint Paul's Cathedral. In 1959 he played Othello one more time, at Stratford-upon-Avon.
But the years of pressure had taken their toll. In 1961, in Moscow, he suffered a breakdown.
He spent much of the next two years in hospitals.
In 1963 he came home to America, and lived quietly, out of public view. His wife Eslanda died two years later.
Paul Robeson died in Philadelphia, on January 23rd, 1976. He was 77.
Years later, Jackie Robinson wrote that he had come to respect him deeply, as a man who gave up his career, his wealth and his comfort to help his people.
In 1995, Paul Robeson was finally named to the College Football Hall of Fame.
In 2004, he appeared on a United States postage stamp.
His father escaped slavery. His teammates broke his nose. His country took his passport, his concerts and his income.
And still, he told Congress that this was his country too, and that he was going to stay.
That was Paul Robeson. Subscribe for more.

notUsed: Mother's death: house fire (Wikipedia) vs stove-fire accident (Encyclopedia.com): said as "a fire at home".
Income: $150,000 to under $3,000 (Wikipedia) vs $104,000 to $6,000 (other accounts): said as "over a hundred thousand ... almost nothing".
Peace Arch crowd: 25,000-40,000 depending on source: said as "tens of thousands".
Truman "abruptly ended the meeting": weaker sources; said as "The meeting was over".
Jackie Robinson's later respect: wording from his 1972 autobiography as quoted by Andscape, The Nation and SABR; paraphrased, not quoted.
Easy to Get: Commons dates it 1947, other catalogues 1944: labelled "1940s". It is footage of Robeson speaking to soldiers, not of the 1956 hearing; the hearing beats use it as illustration only.
1961 suicide attempt and electroconvulsive therapy: true (Wikipedia) but left out; script says "breakdown" and "hospitals".
Stalin Prize 1952: left out for time.
